visual_match: Single panel with both axes logarithmic (log-log), x-axis = frequency rank r (labeled, starting at 1) and y-axis = word frequency f (labeled, counts); a linear-scale plot or semilog plot is a fail.

Rank axis spans roughly 1 to 10^4 (~15,000–20,000 unique lowercase alphabetic types for a Moby-Dick-sized corpus, i.e. ~4 decades) and frequency axis spans ~1 to ~10^4 (top word 'the' ≈ 13,000–15,000 occurrences), so the data covers at least 3 orders of magnitude on each axis.

Empirical data drawn as many points/markers or a dense step-like curve (order 10^3–10^4 plotted points), monotonically non-increasing in rank, not a smooth analytic line and not a handful (<50) of aggregated points.

A fitted/reference straight line of slope ≈ -1 is overlaid on the data, visually distinguishable (different color/dashed) and spanning the fit region, with the fitted exponent s (or slope) annotated numerically in the legend, title, or as text on the axes.

Qualitative shape shows the expected departures: mild flattening/curvature at the extreme head (ranks 1–10) and a flat 'staircase'/plateau of frequency-1 hapax words at the tail (the last decade of ranks), with an approximately straight middle region.
scientific_claim: A numerically estimated exponent is reported (in the figure annotation and/or log) with magnitude near 1 — acceptable range |s| ≈ 0.8–1.3 (typical full-range log-log fit on Moby-Dick gives ≈ 1.0–1.15); a value outside 0.7–1.5 contradicts the claim.

The fit is performed over 'the bulk' of the distribution (e.g. ranks ~10 to ~1000–5000, or explicitly stated head/tail exclusions), and the excluded regions are stated, so the slope is not an artifact of fitting only the extreme head or only the hapax plateau.
Goodness of fit is reported or evident (e.g. R^2 ≳ 0.95 on log f vs log r over the fit range), demonstrating approximate linearity rather than merely asserting it.
The straight-line region visibly extends over at least ~2 decades of rank and ~2 decades of frequency, supporting 'power law across several orders of magnitude' rather than a local slope estimate.
The figure/log does not overclaim exactness: deviations at head and tail are visible or acknowledged, consistent with 'approximate' power law.
implementation: Code reads the actual provided corpus text file from disk and tokenizes it; tokenization uses a lowercase alphabetic rule (e.g. re.findall(r'[a-z]+', text.lower()) or [a-zA-Z]+ then .lower()), with digits/punctuation excluded as specified.
Frequency counting via a dict/collections.Counter over all tokens, then sorted descending to assign ranks 1..N (ties may be broken arbitrarily but ranks must be consecutive integers over all types).

Exponent estimated by an explicit least-squares regression of log(f) on log(r) (e.g. numpy.polyfit(np.log10(r), np.log10(f), 1) or np.linalg.lstsq) over the chosen bulk rank window; slope is taken from the regression output, not assumed.

Sanity statistics printed/logged and plausible for the corpus: total tokens ~2.0×10^5–2.6×10^5, unique types ~1.5×10^4–2.1×10^4, top-ranked token 'the' with count ~1.3×10^4–1.5×10^4, and 'of'/'and' next; grossly different numbers indicate mis-tokenization or truncated reading.

No hard-coded frequency table, no synthetic sampling from a Zipf/zeta distribution used in place of the text, and no arbitrary trimming of the vocabulary before ranking (beyond the documented fit window).
budget_use: Whole pipeline completes well inside the 120 s CPU-only budget (tokenizing+counting Moby-Dick should take ~1–5 s); execution log shows successful termination and a saved figure file, no timeout or partial output.
The full corpus is processed (all lines/characters read), not a truncated prefix or random subsample; token/type counts in the log confirm full coverage.

All unique word types are plotted (no aggressive downsampling that would hide the tail plateau); if downsampling is used for rendering, it is stated and retains ≥10^3 points spanning the full rank range.

Given the generous budget, at least the required deliverables are complete: rank-frequency points, fit over the bulk, annotated exponent, and printed diagnostics (slope, intercept, R^2, fit range); nothing left as a placeholder or TODO.
integrity: Plotted y-values are the empirical counts computed in the script; the reference line is generated from the regression coefficients (10^(intercept) * r^slope), not a hand-drawn or hard-coded 1/r curve masquerading as data.
The annotated exponent in the figure equals the value printed by the regression in the execution log (same number to within rounding); no rounding of a fitted 1.17 down to 'exactly -1'.
No fabricated or paper-copied numbers: the log shows real corpus statistics derived from the file, and the code contains no literal arrays of frequencies or ranks.

Honest labeling: the corpus actually used is named correctly, axes/legend state 'empirical' vs 'fit slope = ...', and any restriction of the fit range or exclusion of hapax legomena is disclosed rather than silently applied to force slope ≈ -1.
No selective deletion of inconvenient regions from the plot (head or tail points must still be shown even if they deviate from the fitted line).
